newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak market sceptical about foreign stock on BSE.
newsitem.headline: Slovak market sceptical about foreign stock on BSE.

text.p: Slovakia's capital market, heavily depressed by a lack of liquidity, stands to get little help from the planned introduction of foreign shares on the local bourse, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Slovak parliament is discussing an amendment to the securities' law permitting the issue and trade of foreign shares on the Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE).
It is expected to give final approval to the law in the autumn but market players remain sceptical.
"I cannot imagine any foreign company launching its share issue on the BSE at the moment," Dusan Sykora of ING Barings told Reuters.
"Lucrative issues simply will not come, as they don't need this narrow market, while those unattractive others will not help even if they do come," Sykora said.
Bourse officials admitted the amendment would be more or less cosmetic bowing to requirements for Slovakia's admission to the OECD, expected at the end of this year.
"Frankly, I don't think foreign issuers would be strongly interested in entering our market in the current situation," BSE general secretary Marian Sasik said.
"But domestic investors are interested in foreign issues, therefore any change in this direction may lead to a better situation," he added.
Trading on the BSE has declined continuously since April, hit mainly by money market turbulence which caused an enormous increase in interest rates.
That compounded the worries of foreign investors who have also been discouraged by general political uncertainty in Slovakia and a lack of new share issues on the market.
The official 16-share SAX index has lost some 20 percent of its value, gradually falling from its year high of 208.64 points on March 21 to current levels of around 167 points.
Sasik said the cause of the current problems on the BSE goes back even further than this spring, as only less then 100 issues, out of total 914, have had any activity at all.

"The coupon privatisation in 1991 resulted in creation of the capital market in this country but the structure of the issues (from the coupon scheme) did not completely fit the market's needs," Sasik said.
"Investors would definitely welcome (new) issues such as the tobacco industry or utilities," Sykora said.

The government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar in 1995 cancelled the second wave of the voucher, or coupon privatisation, replacing it by a bond scheme issued by the National Property Fund (NPF), the state's privatisation agency.

But the new scheme resulted in general disappointment as a significant majority of individual bond holders have either been unable to sell their bonds or have been forced to accept a price far below their nominal 10,000 crowns. -- Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402
